title: Primary Function of the System
learningObjectives: Identify the physical function before developing a mechanics model.
student: What is the primary engineering function of the pipe connection shown in the industry image?
instructor: The pipe transports high-temperature steam or process fluid between connected pieces of equipment while maintaining a sealed mechanical connection.
gradingNotes: Students should identify the physical function before treating the assembly as a spring-supported axial member.

title: Source of Mechanical Loading
learningObjectives: Distinguish thermally induced loading from a directly applied axial force.
student: What change in operating condition can create mechanical loading in the pipe even when no direct axial force is externally applied?
instructor: A temperature increase causes the pipe to expand. If that expansion is restrained, axial forces develop in the pipe and at its connections.
gradingNotes: Students should distinguish a thermally induced load from a directly applied mechanical load.

title: Supports and Restraints
learningObjectives: Explain how connected equipment restrains thermal expansion.
student: How do the connected machines and their supporting structures affect the thermal expansion of the pipe?
instructor: The machines and their supporting structures resist free movement of the pipe ends. Because the supports have finite flexibility, they permit some attachment movement, but the pipe remains partially restrained and develops axial force.
gradingNotes: At this stage, describe the physical restraint without introducing the spring-stiffness symbol.

title: Load Path
learningObjectives: Trace the thermal load from the heated pipe into the supporting structure.
student: Trace the mechanical load path when thermal expansion of the pipe is restrained.
instructor: The heated pipe attempts to expand. Restraint at the connected equipment creates axial force in the pipe. That force passes through the pipe connections into the machine housings and then through their supports into the foundation.
gradingNotes: Use physical component names here rather than labels from the later instructor idealization.

title: Relevant Mechanical Response
learningObjectives: Select the responses supported by the one-dimensional model.
student: What mechanical responses should be evaluated to determine the effect of thermal expansion on the pipe and its connections?
instructor: The analysis should evaluate free thermal expansion, the restraint-induced axial force, axial deformation of the pipe and supports, and the resulting average axial stress in the pipe.
gradingNotes: The base model does not evaluate flange and bolt behavior, pressure stress, bending, creep, or fatigue.

title: Effect of Support Flexibility
learningObjectives: Predict how equipment flexibility affects restrained thermal force.
student: Would a more flexible equipment-support system be expected to increase or decrease the thermal force in the pipe? Explain.
instructor: A more flexible support system decreases the thermal force because greater attachment movement accommodates more of the pipe's thermal expansion.
gradingNotes: This qualitative result prepares students for the spring-supported reference model.

title: Relevant Parameters
learningObjectives: Identify the physical parameters that govern thermal force and stress.
student: What geometry, material, thermal, and support characteristics influence the thermal force developed in the pipe?
instructor: The important characteristics are pipe length and cross-sectional geometry, elastic modulus, coefficient of thermal expansion, temperature change, and the flexibility or stiffness of the connected equipment supports. Pipe yield stress is needed for the limited strength comparison.
gradingNotes: Identify physical dependencies at this stage; the formal symbols and equations are introduced after the transition.

title: Student-Generated Structural Idealization
learningObjectives: Convert the physical system into a one-dimensional mechanics model.
student:
Develop a simplified one-dimensional Mechanics of Materials model that preserves the dominant thermal-expansion load path. Represent the pipe as an axial member and represent the flexibility of the connected equipment using an appropriate idealized support model.

Student model / free-body diagram space
instructor: A suitable model represents the pipe as a uniform axial member between two flexible attachment locations. The student model should show the pipe, two equipment attachments, pipe length, temperature change, support flexibility, and the unknown thermally induced axial force.
gradingNotes: Students should create their model before viewing the instructor reference idealization.

title: Modeling Assumptions
learningObjectives: State assumptions supporting the simplified thermal model.
student: State the assumptions needed to reduce the real pipe-and-equipment system to the simplified model.
instructor: Assume a uniform temperature change, one-dimensional axial response, linear-elastic behavior, small deformation, a constant hollow circular pipe section, linear support flexibility, and rigid flange load transfer. Neglect pressure stress, bending, creep, thermal gradients, detailed bolt and gasket behavior, and flexibility associated with the complete pipe routing.

title: Mechanics Analysis Plan
learningObjectives: Plan the calculation from geometry through engineering assessment.
student: Develop a step-by-step plan for determining the thermally induced pipe force and stress using the simplified model.
instructor: Determine the pipe cross-sectional area; calculate the temperature change and free thermal expansion; write compatibility between free expansion, elastic shortening of the pipe, and movement of both attachment locations; solve for the pipe force; calculate the average axial stress; and make a limited engineering assessment.
gradingNotes: The intended sequence is thermal strain, compatibility, force, stress, and interpretation.

title: Boundary Conditions and Support Idealization
student: Using the instructor reference idealization, describe the boundary conditions and support model at pipe ends A and B.
instructor: The pipe is attached at A and B to two equipment connections, each represented by a linear axial spring of stiffness k. The attachment locations can move under load, so the pipe is partially restrained rather than perfectly fixed.

title: Unknown Thermal Pipe Force
learningObjectives: Identify the unknown interaction force and its direction.
student: Identify the unknown axial force developed in the pipe when its thermal expansion is restrained. State whether the pipe is expected to be in tension or compression for the assigned temperature change.
instructor: The unknown is the thermally induced axial pipe force F. For the assigned temperature increase, the pipe is in {{thermal_force_state}} and applies equal-magnitude forces in opposite directions to the two equipment attachments.

title: Pipe Cross-Sectional Area
learningObjectives: Calculate the material area of the hollow pipe.
student: For Do = {{D_o}} {{D_o_unit}} and t = {{t}} {{t_unit}}, determine the pipe inner diameter and cross-sectional area.
gradingNotes: For the default data, Di = 3.50 in and A ≈ 2.945 in2.

title: Free Thermal Expansion
learningObjectives: Calculate the unrestrained thermal deformation of the pipe.
student: Determine the temperature change and the free thermal expansion of the pipe if both ends were unrestrained.
instructor:
ΔT = T2 - T1 = {{T_2}} - {{T_1}} = {{thermal_delta_T_F}}°F.

δT = αLΔT = {{thermal_free_expansion_in}} in. The positive result represents free expansion.

title: Compatibility Equation
learningObjectives: Write compatibility for a heated member between two flexible attachments.
student: Write the compatibility equation relating free thermal expansion, elastic shortening of the pipe, and movement of both equipment attachment locations.
instructor:
Using F as the positive magnitude of the compressive thermal force,

αLΔT = FL/(AE) + 2F/k.

For the default data, the pipe compliance is {{thermal_pipe_compliance_in_per_kip}} in/kip and the combined attachment compliance is {{thermal_support_compliance_in_per_kip}} in/kip.
gradingNotes: The factor of two is required because both equipment attachments move.

title: Thermal Pipe Force
student: Solve the compatibility equation for the axial force developed in the pipe and state the force magnitude transmitted to each equipment attachment.
instructor:
F = αLΔT/[L/(AE) + 2/k] = {{thermal_pipe_force_magnitude_kip}} kip.

The pipe carries approximately {{thermal_pipe_force_magnitude_kip}} kip in {{thermal_force_state}} and transmits that force magnitude to each equipment attachment.
gradingNotes: For the default data, the expected result is approximately 110.5 kip.

title: Pipe Stress and Yield Comparison
learningObjectives: Calculate average stress and make a limited strength comparison.
student: Determine the average axial stress in the pipe and compare it with the A-36 steel yield stress σy = {{sigma_y}} {{sigma_y_unit}}.
instructor:
σ = F/A = {{thermal_pipe_stress_magnitude_ksi}} ksi in {{thermal_stress_state}}.

The stress is below the specified 40 ksi yield stress, but the yield-to-stress ratio is only {{thermal_yield_ratio}}, so the margin in this limited comparison is modest.
gradingNotes: For the default data, the expected stress is approximately 37.5 ksi in compression. This is not a piping-code acceptance check.

title: Effect of Attachment Stiffness
learningObjectives: Explain how support stiffness changes thermal force.
student: Explain how increasing or decreasing the equipment-attachment stiffness affects the thermally induced force in the pipe.
instructor: Increasing attachment stiffness permits less equipment movement and increases the thermal force toward the fully restrained limit. Decreasing attachment stiffness permits more movement and reduces the thermal force.

title: Engineering Assessment
learningObjectives: Make a concise mechanics-based assessment without overclaiming safety.
student: Use the calculated force and stress to provide a concise engineering assessment. Comment on the effect of equipment flexibility and identify important limitations of the model.
instructor:
The default model predicts approximately {{thermal_pipe_force_magnitude_kip}} kip in {{thermal_force_state}} and an average pipe stress of approximately {{thermal_pipe_stress_magnitude_ksi}} ksi. The stress is below but close to the specified yield stress. Equipment flexibility reduces the thermal force; additional flexibility, pipe-routing changes, or an engineered expansion feature may reduce it further.

A complete evaluation must also consider pressure stress, bending, thermal gradients, creep, fatigue, connection and flange behavior, equipment nozzle-load limits, stability, and applicable piping codes.
gradingNotes: The result supports a limited mechanics assessment only and should not be presented as final service acceptance.
